Burst Monitor · the read from the Friday, November 6 close

Taking Turns

On Thursday the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, its worst day since April 2025. For the week the index lost 2.7%. The typical stock inside it finished the week up. That is not a contradiction. It is the shape this market has had since July, and this week it sharpened: two groups of stocks taking turns, one up while the other is down, on three days out of five. An instrument built to watch how the five hundred move together saw the market's second shared pattern reach a size it almost never reaches, a crowd past the bottom of its swing with nothing behind it, and a new structure arriving at the edge of the market's memory. Here is what it saw, in plain terms, and what it is waiting for when Monday's close is added.

If you are new here · the story so far, in three lines

Since July
When the S&P 500 moves, its stocks usually move together: an up day lifts nearly all of them. Since July the biggest shared move has instead been two-sided, one group rising while another falls. The record back to 2000 has nothing like it for longer than a few weeks. This is month five.
October
The index made a record on October 6, carried by its largest names. Over the next weeks the rally rotated away from them: the AI complex (Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, Meta, Alphabet and the names that trade with them) fell while most other stocks rose. On October 21 the instrument fixed the two groups by name so nothing could be re-sorted after the fact. On October 30 the index's worst day since June landed on the group that was already falling, while the typical stock lost a quarter point.
This week
A broad up day, then the broadest down day of the autumn, then a mirror of it. The question this edition answers is whether Thursday was the market finally moving as one shared pattern, the shape its storms have taken. The answer is no: it was the two groups taking turns, louder.

1 · Whose bad week

The index lost 2.7% in a week its typical stock finished up

Five sessions, three reversals. On Monday the index fell half a percent while 69 of every 100 stocks rose. On Tuesday it rose while 63 fell. On Wednesday three stocks in four rose, the index's best day in three months. On Thursday 85 in 100 fell, its worst since April 2025. On Friday the index rose a third of a percent while 64 of 100 stocks fell. Line the five hundred up by what they did over the five days and the one in the middle gained 0.28%. The index lost 2.68%.

The reason an index and its typical stock can disagree is arithmetic. The S&P 500 is cap-weighted: each company counts in proportion to its market value, so large moves in its ten largest listings, about 37% of the value shown, can pull the index away from what its typical stock did. "Typical" here means the median: the stock in the middle when all five hundred are lined up by their returns. On three of this week's five days the two told opposite stories. On the other two, Wednesday and Thursday, the index and most stocks moved in the same direction.

The week, day by day

each session's return: the index, the median stock of all 500, the rally group and the AI group · the label over each day is the share of the 500 that rose

Hold the two groups the instrument fixed on October 21 and the week sorts itself. The rally group, 314 stocks that had carried October's advance, finished the week up 0.58% at the median, with 57% higher; on Thursday it lost 1.55%. The AI group, 115 stocks including Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, Meta and Alphabet, lost 1.40% on the week and 5.04% on Thursday, when 9 in 100 of its members rose; on Friday it bounced 0.82% while the rally group fell 0.98%. The ten largest companies lost 3.77% on Thursday, none of them up, and gained 0.78% on Friday, seven of ten up. Monday and Tuesday were the same alternation at lower volume.

Each row is the median of its members' own returns, not a portfolio. The two groups are the instrument's October 21 selections by position in the swing (chapter 3), not industry categories, and they do not cover the whole index. The ten are the ten largest cap lines shown: nine companies, with Alphabet trading as two lines.

Thursday was not the usual megacap story. On October 30 the ten largest names accounted for about half of a cap-weighted basket's loss; on Thursday they contributed 1.9 points of a 4.3-point fall and the other 490 names contributed 2.4. Technology lost 6.4% at the median and energy 3.3% with none of its 21 names up, but staples and utilities fell too. It was a down day for everyone and a disaster for the hardware names. Friday reversed only the second half of that sentence.

The split since August 13

the median of each group's return since Aug 13, with the S&P 500 and the median of all 500 · gold ticks = shared crests, explained in chapter 4 · the dashed line is the Oct 6 record

Since the record the gap is wider than it was a week ago. From October 6 the index is down 5.65% while its median stock is up 5.70%, with 69% of members higher. The rally group is up 9.3% at the median, 85% of its names higher. The AI group is down 11.0% and the ten largest down 17.5%. An index with 37% of its value in ten names that have fallen 17% loses ground while most of its members rise, and for five weeks it has. The week added one thing: the two sides are no longer just drifting apart. They are alternating.

Outside the instrument · the analyst's layer, kept separate

The instrument reads prices only, by design. Its job is to say where the pressure and the coordination are, not why. Everything below this line is the analyst's: dated facts, an explanation they are compatible with, one view stated before the outcome, and what would weaken each.

The facts, dated against the sessions. Tuesday Nov 3: the midterm elections, with markets open. Overnight into Wednesday: Democrats were projected to take control of both the House and the Senate; the governors-elect of Texas and Ohio had campaigned against new data centers, one pledging an immediate moratorium. Wednesday: the S&P 500 rose 1.6%, its best day in three months. Thursday: the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite 5.5%; the information-technology sector fell 7.3%, its worst day since March 2020; a gauge of semiconductor stocks fell 12%; on the New York Stock Exchange, decliners outnumbered advancers 2,344 to 416. The coverage attributed the day to a reassessment of the AI build-out after the election. Friday 8:30 am ET: the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 165,000 jobs added in October against 65,000 expected, unemployment at 4.1%, and hourly earnings up 3.1% on the year. Traders moved the odds of a December rate increase to 78%; the Federal Reserve had held at 3.75–4.00% on October 28 with two members dissenting in favor of a hike.

A compatible explanation. The election put a political price on the AI build-out, and the hardware names that carry it took the hit on the first full session after the results, with everything else sold alongside them. Friday's bounce in the same names, against a strong jobs number and rising odds of a rate hike, reads as repositioning rather than a second verdict. The shape fits what the instrument measured: the AI group −5.0% then +0.8%, the rally group −1.5% then −1.0%.

The analyst's view, stated November 4, before Thursday. A post-election rally can lift markets quickly; relief in household finances takes longer, and it is household finances that are stretched. Life has become too expensive for too large a share of the population, and the ordinary pressure releases are not there. Inflation running ahead of job and wage growth does not let a rally stick, whatever the midterm history says. The dated facts that bear on it cut both ways. The long-term unemployed numbered about two million in October, 27.6% of all unemployed, the highest share since late 2021, while the economy still added jobs. The New York Fed reports elevated credit-card balances in serious delinquency, 12.8% of balances 90 days late against 7.6% in 2022, while noting that the flow into new delinquency has been fairly stable for almost two years: strain, not acceleration. The BLS's benchmark revision cut 911,000 jobs from the year to March 2025. The instrument can show how stocks respond to all of this; it has no opinion on the argument.

What would weaken each. Against the AI-reassessment reading: the hardware names bouncing hardest on Friday, and the breadth of Thursday, which reached staples and utilities too. Against the household reading: the continued job gains complicate a claim of immediate labor-market deterioration, while leaving the affordability concern unresolved. Against both: none of it explains the split itself, which began in July, before the election was in view.

2 · Fewer stories, one of them loud

The story count fell. What it fell into is the point.

The instrument's simplest reading takes every stock's daily return over the last 21 sessions and asks how many separate things are going on. The story count is the effective number of independent patterns in those returns. Twenty would mean twenty separate stories. A count collapsing toward three or four means one move has taken over, which is what the market looked like on the way into 2008, March 2020 and the spring of 2025. Since October 14 the count has fallen from 13.6 to 6.5. That fall is real. What it is made of is the opposite of the storm shape.

Two more words. The first pattern is the single biggest shared movement in those returns, usually "the market": on an up day nearly every stock rises. The second pattern is the biggest movement left once the first is removed. Since the groups were fixed on October 21, the second pattern has been the AI group moving on its own: in the current window its stocks move about six times as far along it as the rally group does. A day that rides the second pattern is a day the AI complex did something the rest of the market did not.

The story count since August, with Friday computed in

21-session reader (ink) and 63-session reader (gold), by morning · each morning's reading uses returns through the session before, so the hollow markers are the windows that end on Friday, computed on today's prices

Here is what the fall is made of. The first pattern's share of the market's variation is 32%, which is exactly its long-run middle: half of all sessions since 2000 read higher. The second pattern's share is 18%, and that is the eighth-highest reading of more than 6,600 sessions in the record, in the top tenth of one percent, against a median of 8.5%. The other sessions in that company: the September 2020 technology pullback, early October 2019, the tariff shock of April 3, 2025, and July 10 of this year, the week the present split began. The count did not fall because one pattern took over. It fell because a second one grew to a size the record has shown on only a handful of sessions.

The second pattern's share of the market's variation, 2000 to Friday

21-session reader, every fifth session (ink) with the last 30 sessions daily · gold = the eight readings at or above Friday's · the dashed line is the record's median

Two things keep this in proportion. The slow 63-session reader's count, 12.6, is still above its own long-run middle: October's 19.5 was unusually high, and three weeks have brought it back to ordinary. And the fast reader's 6.5, while below its middle, is nowhere near the levels the storms reached. Fewer stories, not one.

Each day's return across the five hundred can also be asked how much of its shape lay along each pattern, and which way. Half of Thursday's shape lay along the second pattern with the AI complex on the down side, and almost none along the first. Friday lay 18% along the second pattern with the sign reversed, the AI complex up. Wednesday, the broad up day, was the week's one first-pattern day. Thursday was the second story told one way; Friday was the same story told the other.

The market has fewer stories because a second one got loud. On the record, that is a different animal from one story taking over.

3 · The clock face

Two crowds, half a cycle apart, and nothing behind the second

The dial on the first page puts every stock on a clock face by where it is in its own swing. On Friday's reading, 57% of names sat just past the top of their swing and 29% just past the bottom: two crowds, half a cycle apart, with the AI complex and the energy names in the second. The quarter that would hold whatever comes next, stocks climbing back toward a top, holds 3% of the five hundred. On October 15 it held 62%.

How the circle reads. The Phase Dial reads each stock's price against its own 20-session average and turns the result into a position in a swing. Twelve o'clock, home, is a stock that has just finished a run up relative to its average; the right-hand side is the roll down; six o'clock, the trough, a stock that has just finished a run down; the left-hand side is the climb back. Motion is clockwise.

How it is read. Across several days, not from one frame. The question the dial answers well is which way a group is travelling, and how consistently, over the last five or six sessions. Within that sequence, names pull back and jump ahead in ways that are unusual for them, and that is part of the movement being watched: the market's bursts of shared energy are what push a stock off its own pace.

What to hold loosely. A position is not a price direction: the AI group registered past the bottom on the day it fell 5%. And the newest frame is a sketch. Every position is recomputed when the next close arrives, ordinarily Tuesday morning for Monday's close, so the exact place of any one dot on Friday, and the exact day a given name crossed the bottom, are the least precise things on the face. A group's sustained movement across the frames is the most. This edition says which drawing it quotes: the print, what the instrument showed on a given morning, or today's drawing, every day redrawn on Saturday's prices.

Read across the three dates, the face tells one story. Near the record, most of the market was still climbing while the largest companies had already crested and begun to roll down. By October 30 the giants were well down the right-hand side and the rest of the market was arriving at the top behind them. Thursday then turned the whole face in a single session, about 110 names crossing the top and about 75 crossing the bottom on the same day, leaving Friday's two concentrations at opposite stages of the swing. The energy stocks are the clearest example of what the dial shows well. Watched frame by frame over the last two weeks they have marched down the right-hand side and into the trough, consistently, and Friday's frame continues that movement: 18 of the 21 sit just past the bottom, none rising. Their sustained descent into the trough region is clear across these frames; individual positions and crossing dates are less precise.

The four quarters of the swing, May to Friday, in today's drawing

share of the 500 in each quarter of its own swing, one price vintage · gold = just past the top · rust = rolling down · blue = just past the bottom · teal = climbing back · the last column is Friday's print

What stands out, scrubbing back and forth through the frames, is what is missing. The upper-left quarter, where stocks climb back toward a top, has emptied in a straight line: 62% of names on October 15, 40% at the end of October, 24% on Wednesday, 3% on Friday. Three weeks ago six names in ten were on their way back up; now fifteen names are. The rally group is cresting and rolling. The AI group has crossed the bottom but not cleared it: of its 115 names, 75 are just past the trough and seven are rising. There is no second crowd on its way down to join them, and no crowd climbing out ahead of them. That empty quarter is the clearest limit on calling Friday's bounce a recovery.

The ten largest names show the other side of the same method: what a single frame cannot settle. Read across the weeks, their direction of travel is as plain as the energy group's: from just past the top in early October, down the right-hand side, to the bottom region by the end of the month, where they have been circling since. What the frames cannot yet settle is whether they have finished. Every morning since October 21 the dial has printed several of the ten past the bottom, and through last week every redraw put them back on the way down. This week that changed, then changed back: Monday's and Tuesday's prints have mostly survived in today's drawing, the first since the groups were fixed; Wednesday's and Thursday's have not, with Nvidia, Micron and Broadcom drawn back before the bottom while Alphabet and Meta held. Friday's own print puts seven of the ten past the bottom again. Microsoft, Apple and Amazon meanwhile crossed the top midweek; the ten are now two groups rather than one.

The same print, thirteen mornings running

for each saved morning since the groups were fixed: the share of the index's value the dial printed just past the bottom (filled gold), and the share today's drawing of that same morning shows there (hollow) · the labels count how many of the ten largest were past the bottom, printed and in today's drawing

The chart above is why the dial is read for direction and not for the exact dot. Thirteen mornings have printed the giants past the bottom; in today's drawing, two of those mornings keep most of them there and the rest keep few or none. The exact crossing of a name on a given morning is the softest number on the board. The firm observations are the ones that survive every redraw: the two-crowd shape, the market's roll down the right-hand side over three weeks, the AI and energy groups' march to the bottom, and the empty quarter behind them. Whether the AI complex has finished is the one thing the frames cannot yet say; the next build, with Monday's close, is the next look.

4 · The pressure

The release from the float came with a falling index

The instrument's picture of coordination is a map. In the second week of October the whole field floated quiet near the record: five names in five hundred under the market's shared pressure, twenty-six sessions since anything shared had fired. Then the pressure came back, eleven sessions in a row, and the index has fallen since. On Thursday it reached the AI complex for the first time since the split.

The motion map places each stock by two things. Vertically, its pressure: how much of its movement is the market's shared movement, against that stock's own normal. The white line is the floor; below it is above-normal pressure, a stock caught up in what everyone is doing; above it, a stock moving on its own. Horizontally, how closely that stock's pressure follows the marketwide pressure. Pressure is refilled by a shared crest, a session on which at least 51 names reach the top of their own swings together, and decays between them, so a long quiet spell lets the whole field float up. Being low on this map does not mean a stock fell more; the map and the return figures describe different things.

Pressure by group, May to Friday

the average position on the map's vertical axis for the rally group (gold) and the AI group (blue), in today's drawing · below 0 is below the floor, under above-normal pressure · gold ticks = shared crests · hover for how many of each group sit below the floor

Two things happened on the map this week. The rally group kept sinking: 263 of its 314 names are below the floor, their average position the lowest of the year. And, new, Thursday pulled the AI complex partway back into the market's shared motion: two of its 115 names were below the floor on Monday, 21 on Thursday, 18 on Friday. For a month the names that fell hardest had been moving on their own; on Thursday the shared move came for them too, the map's way of saying Thursday was broad. The release from October's float has run alongside a falling index. The question for next week is whether shared pressure keeps spreading while prices fall, or prices improve and participation broadens with them.

The shared-crest count, as printed and as redrawn the next morning

names at the top of their own swings on each session, counted on the instrument's pool of 648 · filled = that morning's print · hollow = the next build's drawing of the same session · the line at 51 is the threshold · Friday's redraw arrives with the next build

The shared-crest count tells the same week from the other side. Every morning's print of the newest day runs low and every redraw lifts it; that held again, but the sizes were new. Wednesday's 85 redrew to 202, the largest shared crest of the autumn, with Apple and Microsoft in it. Then the prints went quiet: Thursday's 20 redrew to 52, a crossing by a single name, and Friday printed 23, below the line. Every shared crest of this run has been led by the rally group; the AI group has never led one.

5 · The memory

Two lookbacks, nearly tied, and a new structure at the edge

The last reading has a time dimension. Every morning the instrument asks over what lookback the market's shared energy is most tightly organized against its drawdown from the high: how far back the market is remembering. Two answers have been nearly tied for a month. This week the question acquired a second, newer picture, and something new arrived at the edge of it.

The sweep runs from 60 sessions to six years. At each lookback it measures how strongly the shared energy and the drawdown move together, letting one lead the other by up to 180 sessions; where the relationship is strongly positive the two are coupled at that memory length, where negative, anti-coupled. The winning lookback is the market's working memory for the day; because the daily winner is noisy, the board also keeps a five-morning median of it, the settled reach. On Friday two coupled ridges, at about ten months (216 sessions) and nineteen (408), stood almost level, and the shorter one won the day by a hair. The settled reach is 408. One thing learned this week says how to read the tie: the two lookbacks are closer together than a routine morning's revision of the data moved the same comparison, so the longer five-day reading remains the reference. Read 408 until 216 prints again.

The memory profile on Friday

the relationship at each lookback, Nov 6 (ink) and Oct 30 (faint gold) · open rings = cells whose best lead or lag sits at the ±180 edge of the search, timing unresolved · shaded = the anti-coupled valley · below 130 sessions the instrument's floor

The surface: the same memory, laid out flat

The profile above is one line, the best lead or lag at each lookback. The instrument also keeps the whole thing: a surface with the lookback up the side, 120 to 600 sessions, and the lead or lag across, −180 to +180. Each cell is colored by the relationship: red where the shared energy and the drawdown move together, blue where they move against each other; the left half is the energy following the drawdown, the right half the energy leading it. Red and blue are signs of a relationship, not market up and market down. The two ridges of the profile are the two red peaks on the left. The surface is new on the board this autumn.

Here is the reading, and it is the analyst's, from watching surface films that span more than five years of reconstructed market history. The movement is readable, and the place to watch is the bottom edge. The moment that matters is the transition: an intact structure of the opposite sign arriving along that edge and moving into the field while the established ridges hold their shape. What the field settles into later, red and blue side by side, is the aftermath; the signal is the beginning, when the opposite first moves in. It is not the only pattern the surface shows, but it is the one that recurs at turns, and this week it appeared again: a defined negative structure arriving at the lower right beneath ridges that did not move.

What the record does and does not yet say. On a 20-year reconstruction, the corner that lit this week is lit about half the time, so a level of 40 cells is ordinary; the arrival after two dark months is what is new. A first numerical test asked a narrower question, whether a threshold crossing in that one fixed corner was followed by anything unusual in the index over the next one to three months, and under that screening condition it did not distinguish subsequent returns or ranges from their baselines. That test did not follow the moving edge, the integrity of the arriving structure or the development of its opposite, and it did not include the first features circled in the February 2020 frame, which sit on the other side of the surface. The transition described here has not been reduced to a rule and tested; the one count that exists does not test the moving-edge interpretation. So the reading stands as a reading: watch the arrival for what it does next. Does the new structure stay coherent and advance, or flicker out? Do the two ridges on the left keep their shape while it does?

6 · What would change this read

Three branches, and the five things that will tell them apart

The board does not have a direction this week. It has two groups taking turns, a second story grown loud, a crowd past the bottom with nothing behind it, shared pressure reaching the AI complex for the first time since the split, and a new structure at the edge of the memory surface. Here are the three ways it can go, and what would tell them apart.

Branch 1Still taking turns

The second pattern stays large while the first stays near its middle; the two crowds hold half a cycle apart and keep alternating; the rising quarter stays empty; shared crests keep coming from the rally group. Month five of rotation, louder. Every session this week fits this branch.

Branch 2One market

The first pattern swells and the story count keeps falling through it; down days ride the market rather than the AI complex; the crowds converge on the dial. That is the shape the record's storms had on the way in. Thursday, for all its size, was not this.

Branch 3The turn

The rising quarter fills from below as the AI crowd climbs back; the giants' crossing survives the next redraw; a shared crest is led by the AI group for the first time; prices improve with participation. The surface's sequence, read alongside prices and the dial, tells this branch from the first.
  1. Friday's dots, redrawn when Monday's close is added.now: seven of the ten largest printed past the bottom · 23 names at the top of their swings, below the 51 line

    Do the giants stay past the bottom, as Monday's and Tuesday's prints did, or get drawn back, as Wednesday's and Thursday's were? Do the energy names keep travelling the same way? Does Friday's 23 redraw to a shared crest, and whose?

  2. Monday's return against the two patterns.now: the window ending Friday reads 6.35 on the fast reader · first pattern 33%, second 18%

    Does Monday ride the second pattern, and which way? Its normal review is Tuesday morning. A string of days along the first pattern is the one thing that would move this read toward branch 2.

  3. The rising quarter.now: 15 of 500 names, 1% of value · 62% of names on Oct 15

    Does anything climb back? The turn, if it comes, shows here first.

  4. Which memory holds.now: 216 and 408 almost level · the settled reach 408

    Does 216 print twice and take the settled reach, or does 408 take the day back? Either way the number to quote is the settled one.

  5. The arrival at the edge of the surface.now: 40 cells on Friday under one vintage, from none a week earlier · five new structures on the ledger's row

    Which sign is arriving; does its edge stay coherent and advance, or flicker out as the January 2020 arrival did after nine sessions; and how do the established ridges respond? Read that sequence alongside prices and the dial.

Observed

  • The week and Thursday by fixed group and value weight; the index and its median stock disagreeing on three of five days.
  • The story count and its first two patterns; the second pattern's share against the record since 2000.
  • The dial on three clocks; the rising quarter's share across the film; thirteen mornings of prints against today's drawing.
  • Pressure by group; the shared-crest prints and their redraws.
  • The memory profile; the surface's new structure; the 2020 sequence, reconstructed.

Interpretation

  • The story count fell because the second pattern grew to an unusually high level, not because one pattern took over.
  • Thursday and Friday were mirror days on the same axis.
  • The two-crowd shape and the groups' direction of travel are firm; the giants' exact crossing is not.
  • Thursday pulled the AI complex partway back under shared pressure.
  • The surface's arrival marks a transition, in either direction; the beginning is the signal.
  • The readings of Thursday's cause and of household finances are the analyst's, not measurements.

Not established

  • A direction, a mechanism, a forecast.
  • That the AI complex or the energy names have finished their run down.
  • How far Friday's dots move when Monday's close is added.
  • That Friday becomes a shared crest, or whose.
  • That the surface's transition pattern works as a rule; it has not been reduced to one and tested.
  • That any outside event caused the split.

The instrument's words

A short glossary

The rally group · the AI group
The two groups the dial placed just past the top and at the bottom of their swings on October 21, held fixed by name since: 314 and 115 stocks. The AI group holds Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, Meta, Alphabet and the names that trade with them. Amazon, Apple and Microsoft are in the rally group.
The ten
The ten largest cap lines among the names shown: nine companies, Alphabet twice. About 37% of the value shown.
First pattern · second pattern · story count
The biggest shared movement in the stocks' daily returns over a window, and the biggest left once the first is removed. The story count is the effective number of independent patterns: the fast reader uses 21 sessions, the slow reader 63. Each morning's reading uses returns through the session before, so a day's own move enters the next morning.
The dial · home · the trough · the quarters
Each stock's price against its own 20-session average, read as a position in a swing. Home is the top, the trough the bottom, motion clockwise. The four quarters are just past the top, rolling down, just past the bottom, climbing back. A position is not a price direction.
A print · today's drawing
The morning's reading of the newest day is its print. When the next session arrives every position is recomputed; "today's drawing" means every day redrawn on Saturday's prices. Both are kept, and this edition says which one it quotes. The dial is read across several frames for sustained group movement; individual positions and crossing dates are less precise.
The map · pressure · the floor
Each stock's participation in the market's shared moves against its own normal (vertical) and how closely its pressure follows the marketwide pressure (horizontal). Below the floor is above-normal pressure. Pressure decays on a 21-session half-life unless a shared crest refills it.
A shared crest
A session on which at least 8% of the instrument's pool, 51 names, reach the top of their own swings together. The newest day's count is a sketch and has revised upward on every morning so far.
The memory · settled reach · coupled
The lookback at which the market's shared energy is most tightly organized against its drawdown from the high, and the five-morning median of the daily winners. Coupled is a positive relationship, anti-coupled a negative one; lag means the energy follows the drawdown, lead that it runs ahead.
The surface · the bottom edge
The memory relationship at every lookback and every lead or lag at once, drawn as a colored field. The bottom edge is its shortest lookbacks.

Reading notes, sources and construction

  • The instrument reads daily closing prices for a pool of about 650 names: the current S&P 500 and the names that have left it during the history, so the record is not survivor-biased. 500 current names are shown on the dial and the map; the shared-crest count uses 648. Every number here is regenerated from the raw price files on prices fb3fe504, Saturday's build of the November 6 close, except the shared-crest prints, which are transcribed from each morning's own build.
  • The story-count figures in chapter 2 use returns through Thursday, the instrument's convention; the window including Friday reads 6.35 on the fast reader with the second pattern at 17.8%, and nothing in the chapter changes. The two memory lookbacks are 216 and 408 trading sessions, at +.904 and +.897 on Friday, a margin of .006; the morning revision between Thursday's build and Friday's moved the 216 reading by .021; the five-morning median is 408. From this week each day's memory reading includes that day's close; the October 30 profile shown is on the same convention. The 20-year surface record was built before that change and labels each frame one session later than the live board would.
  • The narrow count referred to in chapter 5: cells with a relationship below −.45 at lookbacks of 108 to 144 sessions and leads of +50 to +95, with at least 40 paired observations, on one reconstruction of 2006–2026. Median 14 cells; 15 or more on 49.9% of sessions; 40 is the 68th percentile; 50 lit runs of five sessions or more. Arrival = fewer than 15 cells on each of the prior 20 sessions, then 15 or more: 41 arrivals. Index return over the next 21 sessions, median +1.6% (all sessions +1.4%), down 32% of the time (34%); over 63 sessions, +3.7% (+3.7%), down 24% (28%); realized range 4.7% (5.0%) and 9.6% (9.9%). The condition was written after seeing Friday's frame; cells are parts of one surface, not independent observations; the test does not address the transition described in chapter 5.

How this edition was made. Jason Connerty built the instrument, ran its chain on the Friday close, and walked the board across the dial, the map and the surface; the readings of the surface in chapter 5 are his. An independent second read checked each observation against the record and edited a first draft for a reader new to the instrument. Claude (Fable 5.1) ran the numbers and wrote the edition.

A Burst Monitor read · written Sunday, November 8, 2026 from the Friday, November 6 close · a position read on history, never a forecast, not investment advice · the newest day's dial positions and shared-crest count restate when the next session is added; the window ending on Friday is computed on Saturday's prices and can change only through a revision of them.
